factors.label: Real GDP
factors.why: The broadest measure of output. Late and revised, so it confirms a turn more than it signals one.

factors.label: Industrial production
factors.why: Hard output from factories, mines and utilities. The most cyclical part of the economy.

factors.label: Philly Fed manufacturing
factors.why: A timely survey of factory activity, above zero means more firms growing than shrinking. Regional, standing in for the ISM index that FRED does not carry.

factors.label: Philly Fed services
factors.why: Service firms on their own activity. Regional, standing in for the ISM services index. Services are most of US output.

factors.label: Real retail sales
factors.why: Goods spending after inflation. The consumer is about two thirds of GDP.

factors.label: Consumer sentiment
factors.why: The University of Michigan survey of how households feel about their finances and the economy. Leads spending at turning points, noisy in between.

factors.label: Nonfarm payrolls
factors.why: Jobs added each month. The single most market-moving release.

factors.label: Unemployment rate
factors.why: Moves slowly, then quickly. A rise of half a point from its low has marked every recession since 1970.

factors.label: Initial jobless claims
factors.why: New unemployment filings. The timeliest read on layoffs, published every Thursday.

factors.label: ADP private payrolls
factors.why: A private-sector count from payroll records. Arrives two days before the official report.

factors.label: Job openings (JOLTS)
factors.why: Labor demand. Openings fall before hiring does.

factors.label: CPI
factors.why: Headline consumer prices. Drives real incomes and the public mood on inflation.

factors.label: Core CPI
factors.why: CPI without food and energy. A cleaner read on the underlying trend.

factors.label: PPI final demand
factors.why: Prices received by producers. Pipeline pressure that can reach consumers later.

factors.label: PCE price index
factors.why: The Fed's 2% target is written in this index.

factors.label: Core PCE
factors.why: The measure the Fed watches most closely when setting rates.

factors.label: Financial conditions
factors.why: The Chicago Fed index: a blend of 105 measures of risk, credit and leverage. Below zero is looser than average.

factors.label: Baa corporate spread
factors.why: Moody's Baa bond yield minus the 10-year Treasury: the price of the lowest investment-grade credit. Widens when credit stress builds, and its history runs back decades.

factors.label: 10-year real yield
factors.why: The inflation-adjusted cost of long-term money. The discount rate behind growth stocks and gold.

factors.label: 2-year Treasury yield
factors.why: The market's view of where the Fed will be over the next two years.

factors.label: Broad dollar index
factors.why: A stronger dollar tightens conditions for the rest of the world and for US multinationals.

markets.label: S&P 500
markets.note: Earnings follow growth and jobs. Hotter inflation keeps rates high, looser conditions lift multiples.

markets.label: Nasdaq 100
markets.note: Long-duration cash flows, so liquidity and real yields carry double weight.

markets.label: Russell 2000
markets.note: Small caps are more cyclical and more dependent on credit, so growth and liquidity carry double weight.

markets.label: 10-year Treasuries
markets.note: Read as bond prices. Strong activity and, above all, hotter inflation push yields up and prices down.

markets.label: US dollar
markets.note: A US-only read: strength and inflation at home mean a firmer Fed and higher US yields. Currencies are relative, so treat this as half the picture.

markets.label: Gold
markets.note: Driven mostly by real yields and the dollar, with a bid from inflation and from weaker growth.

regime.name: Reflation
regime.blurb: Activity and inflation are both picking up. Tends to favour cyclicals and commodities over bonds.
leanings: Commodities have historically been the best asset class. Stocks still rise but lag the phase before.
Cyclical value has tended to lead, such as industrials and basic materials.
Central banks lean against inflation, so yields tend to rise and the curve to flatten.

views.name: Baa
views.note: Moody's Baa yield minus the 10-year Treasury, the lowest investment-grade rung (BBB on S&P's scale). Long bonds, long history.

views.name: Single-A
views.note: ICE BofA index, ratings averaged across Moody's, S&P and Fitch. Spread over the whole Treasury curve. FRED keeps only three years.

views.name: BBB
views.note: ICE BofA index, ratings averaged across Moody's, S&P and Fitch. Spread over the whole Treasury curve. FRED keeps only three years.

views.name: BB
views.note: ICE BofA index, ratings averaged across Moody's, S&P and Fitch. Spread over the whole Treasury curve. FRED keeps only three years.

views.name: Ladder
views.note: One method on one axis, so the gaps are the price of each step down in quality. BB to BBB is the line between junk and investment grade. ICE BofA indices, of which FRED keeps only three years.

views.name: Both
views.note: Below zero the curve is inverted.

views.name: 10Y minus 2Y
views.note: Below zero the curve is inverted.

views.name: 10Y minus 3M
views.note: Below zero the curve is inverted. This is the slope the recession model reads.

views.name: level
views.note: New York Fed yield-curve model, on each month's average 10-year minus 3-month spread.

views.name: level
views.note: Kim-Wright estimate from the Federal Reserve Board: the extra yield for holding a 10-year bond instead of rolling short bills.
